title: Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services

reading.body:
This is an impersonation fraud in which AI-generated video and fabricated social media profiles were used to imitate a real, named attorney. The failure is not in a deployed AI product from a legitimate company but in the offensive use of generative AI tools by outside actors to create convincing likenesses without the subject's consent. The point of harm is the social media distribution layer, where fake accounts posed as authentic professional profiles and funneled victims toward payment through consumer apps.

The scheme reached scale before it was detected, and detection came only because victims contacted the real attorney's office directly. No platform-side verification or automated authenticity check caught the volume of fake accounts before harm occurred, an anti-piracy contractor removed them only after the fraud was already active. A routine check linking advertised professional credentials to verified identity records, or proactive monitoring by the platforms themselves, would have been the earliest available intervention.

What is not established is who the perpetrators are, whether any have been identified or charged, or whether the victims have recovered any money.

reports.title: Scammers steal identity of renowned Miami attorney to target immigrants on social media
South Florida immigration attorney says AI scammers are using his identity to target immigrants
Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services
Legal resident loses thousands seeking citizenship to AI immigration attorney

summary:
Angel Leal, a South Florida immigration attorney with over 30 years of experience, has become a target of artificial intelligence scammers who are stealing his identity to defraud vulnerable immigrants. Criminals have created hundreds of fake social media profiles and AI-generated videos featuring Leal offering immigration services he never provides, such as promising US residency for $2,200. The scams escalated dramatically in recent months, with fraudsters using WhatsApp to direct victims to send money through payment apps like Venmo and Zelle while exchanging fake contracts.

Leal discovered the scheme when potential clients began calling his office about services advertised on social media. His firm hired an anti-piracy company that has successfully removed nearly 6,500 fake accounts, including 3,500 from TikTok, 2,400 from Facebook, and 544 from Instagram. Leal has changed his personal phone number and plans to contact local and federal authorities to investigate the scams. He is warning immigrants to verify the identity of anyone offering legal services online and to be suspicious of social media advertisements requesting immediate payments.
